documentation.range: The Green Turtle has a circumglobal distribution between 40°N and 40°S, occurring throughout tropical and, to a lesser extent, subtropical waters (Mediterranean Sea and Pacific, Indian and Atlantic Oceans) [Wallace et al. 2010, 2023]. Green Turtles are highly migratory and they undertake complex movements and migrations through geographically disparate habitats.
documentation.population:
Nesting occurs circumglobally, primarily in the tropics (Wallace et al. 2023) (see Figure S1 in Supplementary Information). The largest aggregations of nesting Green Turtles occur in the Southwest Pacific and North Atlantic regions (see Table S1 in Supplementary Information). The current nesting trend of Southwest Pacific Green Turtles appears stable, despite concern about decreased hatchling production. The North Atlantic trend has increased significantly over the past 50 years, and despite an apparent decline in recent years, drives the increasing global trend. Please see Seminoff et al. (2015) and individual subpopulation Red List assessments for more detailed information about Green Turtle populations.

Population Trend
Increasing in some subpopulations and overall globally, decreasing in some subpopulations (see Table S1).
documentation.habitats:
The ecology and habitat of Green Turtles were reviewed by Seminoff et al. (2015), where life history traits for regional populations are also presented where available. The typical life cycle for this species is similar to other species of marine turtle; females lay multiple clutches (~100 eggs/clutch) in a breeding year; eggs incubate for 6–8 weeks and sex of offspring is determined by incubation temperature, with most studies recording female biased offspring sex ratios (Seminoff et al. 2015). Upon hatching, hatchlings leave the nesting beach and spend the first few years in the pelagic zone where they are thought to associate with ocean currents before recruiting to coastal habitats where they adopt a herbivorous diet and mature. Green Turtles are migratory as adults, moving between nesting and foraging sites every 2–4 years to breed and showing high site fidelity and natal philopatry. Being long-lived, there is a paucity of data on life history traits such as longevity and aging, confounded by issues such as tag loss. Data from long-term monitoring sites (e.g. Cyprus, French Frigate Shoals, Hawaii and Heron Island, Australia) are now providing valuable new insights into the life history of Green Turtles (see below).

Generation Length
The IUCN Red List Criteria define generation length to be the average age of parents in a population, i.e. older than the age at maturity and younger than the oldest mature individual; or average age at sexual maturity plus ½ reproductive longevity (IUCN 2024). Although different subpopulations may have different generation lengths, since this information is limited, we adopted the same value for all the subpopulations.

Green Turtles in the wild are estimated to attain maturity at 15–50 years (Avens and Snover 2013), and we considered here 30 years to be equal to or greater than the average age at maturity. Data on reproductive longevity in Green Turtles are limited, owing to tag loss issues and lack of long-term datasets, but are becoming available as long-term monitoring projects themselves age. Tagging studies have documented reproductive histories up to 38 years in Hawaii (Balazs et al. 2015), 32 years in the Mediterranean (Broderick, unpubl. data) and > 40 years at Heron Island and Mon Repos, Australia (C.J. Limpus pers. comm.) but these data are currently limited by the duration of the studies. We considered here, 30 years to be equal or greater than the average reproductive longevity. Therefore, we considered 45 years to be equal to or greater than the average generation length, therefore avoiding underestimation as recommended by IUCN (2024).
documentation.threats:
Green Turtles are highly susceptible to anthropogenic threats including bycatch, direct take and trade (legal and illegal), collision with marine vessels, habitat loss and degradation, pollution, disease and climate change.

Direct take of turtle meat, eggs, and parts has been the most important source of mortality for Green Turtles for centuries. Although this has declined in recent years, it remains a common practice in certain cultures in many parts of the world (Bräutigam and Eckert 2006, Humber et al. 2014, Senko and Burgher et al. 2022). A recent global analysis of all reported 'illegal exploitation'—i.e., the take or trade of turtles against established law in the locality where the take occurred— produced estimates of approximately 44,000 turtles/year over the past decade, most of which were Green Turtles (Senko and Burgher et al. 2022). This analysis also suggested a decline over time in the illegal take of turtles, although a review of legal turtle harvests (Humber et al. 2014) found that at that time at least 42 countries and territories permitted direct take of turtles, and the primary species used was Green Turtles (>80%).

Industrial and small-scale artisanal fisheries inflict severe impacts on sea turtles (Wallace et al. 2013a). In particular, small-scale fisheries occur primarily in developing nations with limited capacity and resources to obtain data, and where fisheries management is limited or non-existent, thus hindering comprehensive evaluations of the impacts of incidental capture of marine wildlife. Weak governance, poverty, and a lack of resources for local fisheries managers means that scant attention is devoted to assessing impacts of bycatch on sea turtles. Sea turtles get captured in coastal fishing gear most commonly in gillnets, longlines and trawl nets (Wallace et al. 2013a). Industrial-scale fisheries also incidentally capture Green Turtles and other sea turtle species; conservation resolutions approved by inter-governmental regional fisheries management organizations need to be adequately observed, enforced, and monitored over time to implement intended conservation benefits.

Climate change is known to influence migratory patterns and breeding success of sea turtles (Patricio et al. 2021), and a recent study in the Great Barrier Reef, Australia—home to the world's most abundant Green Turtle subpopulation—revealed feminization and highly skewed sex ratios attributed to impacts of climate change (Jensen et al. 2018). As long-lived reptiles with temperature-dependent sex determination, all marine turtles are vulnerable to change in climate, in particular the effect of rising temperatures on offspring sex ratios and lowered hatching or reduced hatchling fitness (Patricio et al. 2021). The increased incidence of hypothermic stunning, which killed thousands of Green Turtles in Texas during the winter of 2020–2021, is suggested to be linked to range shifts of foraging Green Turtles increasing their abundance in Texas inshore waters.

Habitat loss and degradation is a continuing threat for marine turtle populations both at sea from anthropogenic activities such as fisheries and through coastal development (Biddiscombe et al. 2020). The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) predicts that as sea levels rise in the next 100 years, coastlines will migrate landwards, and increased development of anthropogenic structures will further reduce beach availability for marine turtles (Biddiscombe et al. 2020). With coastal development comes light pollution and the impacts of artificial light at night include significantly decreased survival of hatchlings and disruption of nesting females (Biddiscombe et al. 2020). Plastic pollution degrades marine turtle habitat both at sea and on land and we have yet to understand the implications of ingestion of plastics on reproduction and longevity of marine turtles (Duncan et al. 2015).

Green Turtle Fibropapilloma (GTFP) disease is prevalent in many populations worldwide, and has been shown to be more prevalent in areas with lower water quality (Van Houtan et al. 2014), typically associated with coastal development. Although GTFP does not seem to be a current major threat, disease virulence may be enhanced with predicted climate change (Patricio et al. 2021).

Threats across the different regions are varied and more detail can be found in the regional subpopulation assessments. For more details about threats to Green Turtles globally, see Seminoff et al. 2015.
documentation.measures:
Green Turtles are afforded legislative protection under a number of treaties and laws. Annex II of the Protocol Concerning Specially Protected Areas and Wildlife (SPAW) to the Cartagena Convention; Appendix I to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES); and Appendices I and II of the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS). A partial list of the International Instruments that benefit Green Turtles includes the Inter-American Convention for the Protection and Conservation of Sea Turtles, the Memorandum of Understanding on the Conservation and Management of Marine Turtles and their Habitats of the Indian Ocean and South-East Asia (IOSEA), the Memorandum of Understanding on ASEAN Sea Turtle Conservation and Protection, and the Memorandum of Understanding Concerning Conservation Measures for Marine Turtles of the Atlantic Coast of Africa. In addition, targets set through instruments such as the Convention for Biodiversity (CBD) have led to an increase in the designation of marine protected areas, affording protection of some key Green Turtle nesting and foraging habitats, although the protection of pelagic life stages and migratory corridors remains more of a challenge (Haman et al. 2010, Rees et al. 2016).

As a result of these designations and agreements, together with community actions and interventions, many of the intentional impacts directed at sea turtles have been lessened. Harvest of eggs and adults has been slowed at several nesting areas through nesting beach conservation efforts and an increasing number of community-based initiatives are in place to slow the take of turtles in foraging areas. Fisheries bycatch mitigation methods include the use of Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs), which are the most efficient bycatch reduction device for shrimp trawlers (NRC 1990) and other mitigation methods and implementation of best practices for handling and release of turtles incidentally captured in fishing gear have proved successful in reducing bycatch impacts (e.g., Gilman et al. 2009, Yan et al. 2024). Regional fisheries management organization (RFMO) recommendations are compulsory for their implementation by members, particularly those dealing with tuna fisheries. However, despite these advances, human impacts continue throughout the world. The lack of effective monitoring in fisheries operations still allows substantial direct and indirect mortality, and the unsustainable development of coastal and marine habitats threatens to destroy the supporting ecosystems of long-lived Green Turtles.

Minimising disturbance to mating and nesting turtles and their offspring remains a priority. Conservation actions include restricting boat use in mating and nesting areas to minimize disturbance and reduce the risk of boat strike; the use of best practice lighting design to reduce hatchling misorientation, screening or caging of clutches left in situ to reduce predation, and nocturnal anti-poaching patrols, among other measures. Relocation of clutches under threat of predation, inundation, direct take or light pollution is a common mitigation method across sea turtle programmes. Clutches may be relocated to a higher location within a beach or to beach hatcheries. With the increasing threat of inundation from both sea level rise and increased storminess, clutch relocation may be a valuable tool to mitigate the impacts of future climate but the potential negative impacts of this practice on offspring phenotype and fitness need to be assessed.

Continued monitoring of all Green Turtle life stages is of course important if we are to evaluate the impacts of threats and develop mitigation strategies. Owing to the challenges of monitoring populations at sea there is often, however, a lack of data on the status of foraging populations, both adult (especially males) and juvenile Green Turtles. Similarly, we have a poor understanding of the demographics of Green Turtle populations with many key life history traits poorly described (Hamann et al. 2010). It is important for both foraging and long-term life history studies to continue if we are to understand and mitigate the impacts of threats on this species.

Conservation actions are varied across the different regions, depending on the prevailing threats and more detail can be found in the regional subpopulation assessments.

This assessment only uses breeding females and their nesting activities as indicators of population abundance and as such we urge caution. The rise in many subpopulations presented here is a result of decades of positive action and a reduction of some threats. This species remains conservation dependent and we strongly recommend that conservation actions that have proved successful are continued.
documentation.rationale:
The Green Turtle (Chelonia mydas) is globally distributed throughout the tropical, subtropical and temperate regions of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans and Mediterranean Sea (Wallace et al. 2023; Figure S1A in Supplementary Information). The global population is comprised of 11 subpopulations—North Atlantic, Mediterranean, South Atlantic, Southwest Indian Ocean, North Indian Ocean, East Indian-West Pacific, Southwest Pacific, West Central Pacific, South Central Pacific, Hawaii (North Central Pacific), and East Pacific—that correspond to 'regional management units' (RMUs) (Figure S1B in Supplementary Information) (Wallace et al. 2023), and for which regional assessments have been completed or are underway (Table S1 in Supplementary Information). Green Turtle subpopulation delineation was initially based on Seminoff et al. (2015) designation of 'distinct population segments' (DPSs) under USA's Endangered Species Act. These DPSs provided the initial basis for updates to Green Turtle regional management units (RMUs; Wallace et al. 2023), which were used as subpopulations in Red List assessments. Because some subpopulation assessments were based on the 2015 DPSs and some on 2023 RMUs, there are slight differences in boundaries and overlaps between some adjacent subpopulations (e.g., North and South Atlantic). Nonetheless, this assessment includes information from all Green Turtle subpopulations globally.

The Green Turtle global population extent of occurrence, area of occupancy and number of mature adults exceed all threatened categories under criteria B, C, and D, and no population viability analysis has been conducted (criterion E). To evaluate criterion A, past and present values for a common index of abundance (annual abundance of nesting females or egg clutches) were compiled for all subpopulations based on recent Red List assessments for some individual subpopulations (Table S1 in Supplementary Information) and available information for others, and then analysed for potential long-term declines. The long-term global trend in average annual abundance of clutches at index nesting sites (i.e., sites with consistent long-term monitoring and data availability) appears to have increased 28% (from past value of ~419,000 clutches/yr to recent value of ~526,000 clutches/yr in 2024; see Table S1), thus resulting in a Least Concern listing for the global Green Turtle population under criterion A2b. However, current abundance is likely depleted relative to historical (>200 years ago) abundance, threats persist and imperil multiple subpopulations, and several subpopulations are currently assessed as threatened or Near Threatened under IUCN Red List threatened categories. Thus, conservation efforts must continue to ensure that status improvements persist.

Green Turtles have been affected by multiple stressors across the species' global distribution, including fisheries bycatch, loss and degradation of nesting beaches and foraging areas, pollution, diseases (e.g. fibropapillomatosis), and potentially climate change (Wallace et al. 2011). For centuries, Green Turtles have been subject to direct take (also referred to as harvest or exploitation) by humans around the world for meat, eggs, and other products, both within and outside of legally permitted regimes (Bräutigam and Eckert 2006, Humber et al. 2014). Direct take has generally declined over time, and has often been replaced by legal protections in many countries, but remains a source of mortality in many places (Senko and Burgher et al. 2022).

These multiple stressors reduced Green Turtle abundance around the world through the late 20th century, to the point where the global population was listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List due to a 48% to 67% decline over time (Seminoff 2004). However, the recent update indicates that the global population has increased ~28% from past values (mostly 1970s and 1980s, but earlier in some places) to estimated 2024 values (see Table S1). Thus, despite multiple, consistent, and in some cases increasing (e.g., climate change impacts) threats, conservation efforts to protect nesting females and their eggs, and those to reduce harvest pressure, have been successful in many places around the world.

However, Red List assessments of the risk of imminent global extinction in the wild of a widespread species like the Green Turtle—and marine turtles in general—have long been recognized as having little utility for conservation and little justification from a population dynamics perspective, given the complex population structures and biological variation among regional populations of marine turtle species (Mrosovsky 2003, Godfrey and Godley 2008, Seminoff and Shanker 2008). For these reasons, in the past decade, the IUCN SSC Marine Turtle Specialist Group has produced subpopulation-level assessments for multiple marine turtle species, and continues to emphasize the biological and conservation relevance of these assessments in comparison to the global, species-level assessments.

Abundance increases highlighted in this assessment and those of individual subpopulations are likely due in large part to conservation and legal protections, thus making the current improved status of several subpopulations—and the global population overall—dependent upon the continued and improved conservation efforts. Observed abundance increases are non-uniform and uneven; several subpopulations are listed under threatened (and Near Threatened) categories on the Red List, some because of declining trends, others because of geographic range restrictions (Table S2). In addition, despite apparently stable numbers of nesting females and clutches in the Southwest Pacific subpopulation, which is the world's most abundant Green Turtle subpopulation, low clutch success and hatchling production is a major cause of concern for the persistence of this subpopulation (Booth et al. 2018, 2020; Hamann et al. 2025). Further, the subpopulation with second-highest abundance, the North Atlantic, has increased significantly over time and is currently Least Concern (criterion A2b; Lagueux et al. 2025). However, the trend at Tortuguero (Costa Rica), the largest nesting site for the North Atlantic, has shown a concerning decline since 2008 through 2023 (Restrepo et al. 2023). Other subpopulations (e.g., Hawaii, USA) may be suffering from loss of critical habitat (Chaloupka and Pilcher 2019) that could cause a change in Red List status in future assessments.

Moreover, though increasing overall, Green Turtle abundance globally and at most subpopulation scales is considered significantly depleted relative to centuries ago, before commercial harvest regimes were developed (McClenachan et al. 2006). This 'shifting baseline' phenomenon is considered to be somewhat common to marine turtle Red List assessments, as long-term, quantifiable data are typically unavailable to permit robust analysis of trends going back several generations, which for marine turtles typically span multiple decades. Thus, it is important to recognize that the trends presented in this assessment reflect available information from the most recent decades only, and though encouraging, it is unlikely that any subpopulation has achieved historical abundance levels, even within an order of magnitude. 

Criterion A. Reduction in population size
We used the following approach taken for the recent Red List assessments for Loggerhead turtles (Casale and Tucker 2017) and Leatherback turtles (Wallace et al. 2013b) to apply criterion A.

For marine turtles, annual counts of nesting females and their egg clutches (more often the latter) are the most frequently recorded and reported abundance metric across index monitoring and conservation sites, species, and geographic regions (National Research Council 2010). Given that this assessment does not take account of other life stages and nesting occurs outside of index sites, sometimes in significant numbers (see Mortimer et al. 2020), the abundance numbers presented in this assessment should not be interpreted as total subpopulation or global abundance of the species. These counts can be converted from clutches to numbers of females and vice-versa based on biological studies and an understanding of average numbers of clutches per female, to standardize data sets across sites. We used numbers of clutches per year as a measure of abundance in calculating criterion A.

To apply criterion A, three generations (or a minimum of ten years, whichever is longer) of abundance data are required (IUCN 2024). The challenges of this requirement on long-lived species like turtles—with generation lengths of 30 yr or more—are obvious (see Seminoff and Shanker 2008 for a review). Abundance data from ~135 yr ago (one generation estimated 45 yr; see Habitat and Ecology section) are not, however, available for any turtle population in the world. Extrapolating backward using population trends estimated with current datasets was an approach used in previous marine turtle Red List assessments, including that of the Green Turtle (Seminoff 2004). This approach is now considered inappropriate because estimates produced would be biologically unrealistic and unsubstantiated, given what is currently known about sea turtle nesting densities on beaches and other factors (e.g. Mrosovsky 2003).

In the absence of long-term data, we assumed that population abundance three generations ago (~135 years), was similar to the first observed abundance rather than assuming that the population has always been in a decline (or increase). This approach also has obvious flaws, but we assert that this key assumption about historical abundance is a more conservative approach, and does not produce unrealistic values of historical abundance, particularly for those subpopulations with declining trends. Thus, to apply criterion A, we assumed that the abundance at the beginning of an available time series dataset had not changed significantly in the preceding three generations, and therefore used the same abundance value in trend calculations. Past values in most datasets date to the 1970s and 1980s, but some started in the late 1800s and early 1900s. For the Green Turtle subpopulation assessments, we only considered time series datasets of ≥10 yr, and the subpopulation-level datasets were used to estimate long-term trends for the global population (see Table S1). However, it should be noted that Green Turtles typically show much greater inter-annual variation in nesting numbers in comparison to other marine turtle species, creating greater error around estimates and projections. Past population abundance estimates were taken as the multi-year average (three to five years, as data allowed) following commencement of records for each index nesting beach. Multi-year estimates were necessary because Green Turtles are non-annual breeders and there is high inter-annual variation in cohort abundance (and thus clutch abundance). Because the most recent year for available abundance data within and across subpopulations varied between 2015 to 2023, we estimated the numbers of clutches laid at each rookery through 2024 based on the linear extrapolation of each subpopulation's annualized trend based on data from available years. From one past and one recent abundance value (each representing the annual average of three to five-year clutch estimates, depending on data availability), we calculated annual and overall trends (past abundance versus present abundance) for each subpopulation based on abundance data reported in each subpopulation Red List assessment, and then calculated the overall global population trend by weighting each subpopulation trend by its past abundance estimate.

Globally, Green Turtle average annual clutch abundance at index nesting beaches with ≥ 10 years of monitoring data has increased from a past value of ~419,000 clutches/year to ~526,000 clutches per year, indicating a ~28% increase (see Table S1), and thus a Least Concern status under criterion A. Subpopulation-level trends range from ~20% to ~50% decreases (East Indian/West Pacific, North Indian, East Pacific subpopulations) to >200% increases, particularly for the South Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea subpopulations (Table S1). In particular, the North Atlantic subpopulation has increased >130% since the 1980s, and because it is the second-most abundant in the world, this trend largely drives the global trend. However, significant reductions in offspring production over the past 10+ years in the most abundant subpopulation—the Southwest Pacific—belies its apparently stable current trend in nesting activities by adult females, raising concerns about this subpopulation and thus the global population in the future (Hamann et al. 2007; Booth et al. 2018, 2020; Smithers and Dawson 2023).

Further, historical abundance of Green Turtles across subpopulations was almost certainly significantly higher than even the highest present abundance values in Table S1, and perhaps higher by at least an order of magnitude at subpopulation scales (McClenachan et al. 2006). However, available information is insufficient for inclusion in Red List assessments for various reasons; for example, catch and harvest data are reported as numbers or tonnage of turtles, with no indication about age, sex, or maturity status that would allow for conversion to adult female equivalents for purposes of comparing with present day indices of abundance. Nonetheless, several examples exist that clearly illustrate high abundance historically of green turtles in places where they might be increasing, but still at much lower abundance levels. For instance, historical catch data from the eastern Mediterranean suggest that "at the height of the season some 600 specimens were caught a day, 90% of them Chelonia", (Sella 1982). Though increasing, recent estimates of annual clutches laid for the entire Mediterranean subpopulation is ~6,000 clutches/year (Table S1).

In another example, analyses of historical records from the period of invasion of the western hemisphere by European explorers and settlers suggest that Tortuguero, Costa Rica—now the second largest Green Turtle rookery in the world whose increasing trend is driving the North Atlantic subpopulation trend and global trend—might have hosted >100,000 nesting females per year; presently, ~70,000 egg clutches are laid per year at that site (McClenachan et al. 2006; Restrepo et al. 2023). Historical estimates of total adult abundance of the entire Caribbean region range from 33 to 91 million turtles (McClenachan et al. 2006). Using average clutch frequency of three per female per season, and average remigration interval (i.e., years between consecutive breeding seasons; Green Turtles are not annual breeders) of three years means that the estimates of annual clutches laid averaged across three to five seasons will be similar to estimates of the total abundance of adult females. Thus, the present abundance of adult females in the North Atlantic subpopulation might be at least two orders of magnitude lower than it once was.

While we were unable to quantify these historical data under IUCN Red List Guidelines and Criteria, we highlight the 'shifting baseline' phenomenon underlying the Least Concern result of the present assessment. The present increasing abundance trends are certainly encouraging, and show that sea turtle conservation works, when implemented effectively and persistently. Results also show that Green Turtle populations have withstood heavy pressure from multiple sources of mortality over time through the present and are responding robustly to those conservation efforts. However, those stressors likely reduced Green Turtle numbers significantly, making current abundance but a small fraction of what abundance once was centuries ago. Whether present-day conditions and the quality of available habitat could support restored Green Turtle populations at historical levels of abundance is unknown, but unlikely. Nonetheless, it is clear that—while Green Turtles are not at risk of extinction—their numbers remain dramatically reduced relative to historical levels, and their current status is dependent upon recent, ongoing, and continued conservation. 

Criterion B. Geographic range
Extent of occurrence (EOO) of the global Green Turtle population exceeds the thresholds for all threatened categories (>20,000 km2). For marine turtles, nesting habitat is used to calculate area of occupancy (AOO); similar to EOO, total AOO for the global Green Turtle population exceeds thresholds for all threatened categories (> 2,000 km2). Based on these criteria, Green Turtles are Least Concern under criterion B.

Criterion C & D. Population size of mature individuals
Criteria C and D relate to numbers of adults at the global scale. However, data collected for Green Turtle subpopulations that we used in this assessment were reported in the number of egg clutches per year. Marine turtles do not nest annually, and here we used a conservative remigration interval value of three years to obtain an estimate of adult females. Given that sea turtles deposit multiple clutches of eggs in each nesting season, and the average number of clutches laid by individual females per season ranges between three (Hirth 1997) to six (Weber et al. 2013) across subpopulations, we estimate a range in the number of nesting females globally. Therefore, the number of clutches laid annually was estimated to be ~526,000 clutches/year, which corresponds to approximately 263,000 to 526,000 adult females. This value exceeds the thresholds for all threatened categories. Thus, the Green Turtle global population is Least Concern under criteria C and D.

Criterion E. Quantitative analysis of the probability of extinction
A formal quantitative analysis of the probability of extinction of the global Green Turtle population has not been conducted.
